analysis.title: Weekly Economic Commentary: The Fed Is Behind The Curve / Spain Sets Its Course / China: Closer to Japanification?
key_insights: Northern Trust argues the Fed is behind the curve on inflation. Officials expect orderly disinflation but inflation has stayed high, and household surveys show expectations are less anchored than the Fed Chair states.
Serial price shocks since early 2025 (tariffs, the war in Iran raising fuel and shipping costs, AI buildout input pressure) make inflation look more persistent in both data and perception.
An increasing share of CPI items are rising by more than 3%, which the report reads as broadening inflation similar to the post-COVID miscalculation.

Market-based inflation compensation (a Fed gauge) shows low and stable expectations, but the report says it may give a false sense of security. Survey measures are higher and proved prescient in 2021.
Hourly earnings are failing to keep pace with current and forward inflation, which may add wage pressure in the pipeline.
The Fed raised rates in September 2026 and held in October. The report says more hikes may be needed, and markets price three more 25bp hikes by mid-2027.
Legislative responses to affordability concerns after the midterms are unlikely to bend the cost curve much, leaving the Fed with the main influence on inflation.
Spain votes November 29 with the EU effectively on the ballot. Polling is too close to call, and the report says the next government may turn inward, away from the EU.
Spain's October inflation hit a three-year high of 4.9% on energy costs. Growth above the eurozone average, aided by immigration, has kept debt sustainable and avoided a French-style bond selloff.
Spain faces 10% US tariffs on most exports and 15% on autos, plus Chinese competition in autos. Sánchez's criticism of Trump has not provoked retaliation.
Elections in France, Estonia, Finland, Greece, Slovakia, Poland and Italy follow next year, and Spain may be a harbinger for them.
China looks closer to Japanification than a few years ago. Dwelling investment is down about 30%, new construction down about 80% over five years, and mortgage lending fell 4.1% YoY.
China's PPI producer goods rose from -0.6% YoY in February to 7.2% in October, driven by six energy-related industries (over 80% of October's monthly PPI increase). CPI remains below 1%.

China has offsets Japan lacked: a large export machine, state control of the financial system, and AI and automation productivity scope. Risks include delayed loss recognition and automation suppressing wages.

macro_indicators.interpretation: Three-year high driven by energy costs, adds to European inflation and policy pressure.
Markets price further tightening, consistent with the report's view that the Fed may need to hike again.
Reflects upstream energy input costs rather than demand strength.
Continued property-sector balance sheet weakness resembling Japan post-1990.
Deflation risk persists despite producer price rise.

macro_indicators.reading: hike in September, hold in October
macro_indicators.interpretation: Fed has begun tightening but is seen as behind the curve.

risk_factors: Inflation persistence and broadening could force more Fed hikes.
Unanchored household inflation expectations and wage pressure.
Spanish election outcome shifting policy away from the EU.
Populist gains in upcoming European elections.
China balance-sheet recession, weak consumption and deflation risk.
Automation outpacing job creation in China suppressing wages.
Delayed loss recognition from state-directed adjustment in China.
charts_described: Chart of median FOMC PCE inflation expectations for 2026 and 2027 shows 2026 projections rising across Sep-25 to Sep-26 (labels include 2.6%, 2.4%, 2.7%, 3.6%, 3.7%) while 2027 labels stay near 2.1% to 2.5%.
Chart of China GDP per capita shows China at 13,862 and Japan at 35,951 in current dollars.
geopolitical: War in Iran has raised fuel and shipping costs and contributed to price shocks.
Ukraine and Iran conflicts hit European energy costs, with Spain weathering them better than peers.
US tariffs of 10% on most EU exports and 15% on autos apply to Spain.
European Commission is reviewing Chinese trade practices.
Spain's immigration regularization of up to one million migrants and the Ceuta and Melilla migrant surge drive populist tension.
Spanish election November 29 and a wave of 2027 European elections raise EU cohesion questions.

tension_points.bull_case: The Fed sees inflation declining in an orderly way and market-based long-term expectations are low and stable, justifying a hold after the September hike.
tension_points.bear_case: Household surveys show higher expectations, more CPI items rise above 3%, and wages lag inflation, so the Fed may need further hikes.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Not explicitly stated, though a continued hold despite broadening CPI and rising survey expectations would confirm the behind-the-curve view.

tension_points.bull_case: China has export strength, greater productivity scope from AI and strong state control over finance, which lowers financial crisis risk.
tension_points.bear_case: Property correction, shrinking population, weak retail sales and deflation risk resemble Japan after 1990, and state control may delay loss recognition.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Report says watch whether advantages offset structural drags before weak demand becomes entrenched.

theme_stances.key_argument: Inflation has stayed stubbornly high and the Fed may need to raise rates again in upcoming meetings.
theme_stances.evidence: All of this suggests that the Fed may need to raise rates again

theme_stances.key_argument: China looks closer to Japanification than a few years ago but has advantages Japan lacked.
theme_stances.evidence: China today looks closer to Japanification than it did a few years ago
